name: Rice leaf blast
cues: Spindle-shaped spots with brown margins and gray centers.
care: Review water and fertilizer management. Avoid dense growth.
prevention: Choose resistant varieties and manage infected residue after harvest.
limitations: Preliminary visual screening only; similar symptoms may have other causes.

name: Rice bacterial leaf blight
cues: Water-soaked stripes along leaf margins that enlarge and yellow.
care: Reduce plant injury. Review fertilization and water management, and control weeds.
prevention: Use healthy seed and resistant varieties.
limitations: Preliminary visual screening only; similar symptoms may have other causes.

name: Corn common rust
cues: Golden to cinnamon-brown pustules on both leaf surfaces, darkening with age.
care: Record dated changes and photographs for continued observation.
prevention: Consider resistant or tolerant varieties for subsequent planting.
source: Pacific Northwest Pest Management Handbooks · March 2026
limitations: Preliminary visual screening only; similar symptoms may have other causes.

name: Brown planthopper / hopper damage
cues: Visible planthoppers near rice stems, with patches of drying brown plants in heavy infestations.
care: Inspect the base of plants and monitor affected patches. Avoid indiscriminate insecticide use, which can contribute to outbreaks.
prevention: Use locally suitable resistant varieties and discuss water management and pest counts with agricultural staff.
source: Sri Lanka Department of Agriculture · Rice Research and Development Institute
limitations: Brown or drying leaves alone cannot identify a planthopper. A close-up of the insect is needed for a possible pest match.

name: Fall armyworm
cues: A visible caterpillar with a pale inverted Y on the head and four dark spots forming a square near the rear; feeding damage and frass may be present in the whorl.
care: Scout maize plants and inspect whorls for larvae and frass. Confirm larval identity before choosing control measures.
prevention: Monitor regularly and preserve natural enemies; use an integrated pest-management approach with local guidance.
source: CABI · Community-based fall armyworm management training manual
limitations: Holes or frass alone cannot confirm fall armyworm. The larval identifying features must be visible.

name: Citrus canker
cues: Raised, corky brown lesions with water-soaked margins and a yellow halo on leaves, fruit, or stems.
care: Keep potentially infected plants and clippings on site. Ask local agricultural staff to assess the tree; there is no curative treatment for canker.
prevention: Use healthy nursery stock and avoid moving potentially contaminated plants or equipment.
limitations: Photo screening suggests possibilities. Confirm the cause with local agricultural assistance before choosing a treatment.

name: Citrus leafminer damage
cues: Winding mines beneath the surface of young leaves, often with curling or distorted new growth.
care: Inspect tender new leaves and record the extent of mining. Preserve predators and parasitoids.
prevention: Avoid excessive flush growth from unnecessary fertilization or watering; discuss local timing with an agricultural adviser.
source: NSW Department of Primary Industries · Citrus leafminer
limitations: Mines can support a preliminary damage match; a photo does not establish the pest population or treatment need.

name: Okra yellow vein mosaic symptoms
cues: A network of yellow veins enclosing green leaf tissue; later yellowing and stunting can occur.
care: Check for whiteflies and ask an agricultural adviser to assess suspected virus-affected plants.
prevention: Use locally suitable resistant varieties and manage whitefly vectors as part of an integrated plan.
source: National Horticulture Board, India · Okra diseases
limitations: A photograph cannot confirm a virus. The result describes a possible symptom pattern, not a laboratory diagnosis.

name: Whiteflies
cues: Tiny white winged adults or scale-like nymphs on leaf undersides, sometimes with honeydew or sooty mold.
care: Inspect leaf undersides, remove isolated infested leaves, and use yellow sticky traps for monitoring.
prevention: Inspect new plants and protect beneficial insects; avoid unnecessary broad-spectrum insecticide use.
limitations: The insects should be visible. Yellow leaves alone do not identify a whitefly infestation.

name: Eggplant Cercospora leaf spot
cues: Angular or irregular pale lesions that become gray-brown; heavily affected leaves may drop.
care: Record affected leaves and remove affected plant material using appropriate farm sanitation.
prevention: Inspect plants regularly and maintain field sanitation; seek local advice before chemical management.
source: National Horticulture Board, India · Brinjal diseases
limitations: Photo screening suggests possibilities. Confirm the cause with local agricultural assistance before choosing a treatment.

name: Eggplant shoot and fruit borer damage
cues: Bored shoots or fruits, frass-filled entry holes, and wilted shoots; a larva may be visible inside affected tissue.
care: Remove infested plant parts and ask local agricultural staff about integrated control and suitable natural enemies.
prevention: Inspect shoots and fruits regularly so infestations can be found early.
source: World Vegetable Center · Home garden crop guides
limitations: A damaged fruit alone is suggestive. Include entry holes, frass, and any visible larva in a close-up.

name: Chili anthracnose
cues: Small water-soaked fruit lesions becoming dark and sunken, sometimes with rings; affected branches can die back from their tips.
care: Remove affected plant parts and record any additional affected fruits.
prevention: Maintain sanitation and use local agricultural advice for a crop-specific management plan.
source: ICAR Central Coastal Agricultural Research Institute · Vegetable production bulletin 36
limitations: Photo screening suggests possibilities. Confirm the cause with local agricultural assistance before choosing a treatment.

name: Thrips on chili
cues: Tiny slender insects on tender growth; associated leaves or buds may be bronzed, curled, or distorted.
care: Inspect new growth and use good sanitation to remove old flowers, weeds, and infested debris.
prevention: Inspect incoming plants and protect natural enemies by avoiding unnecessary broad-spectrum sprays.
source: University of California IPM · Chilli thrips
limitations: Thrips species cannot reliably be confirmed from a field photo. This entry supports only a possible thrips-group observation; leaf curling has other causes.

name: Sweetpotato feathery mottle symptoms
cues: Mottled leaves, yellow spots with possible purple margins, or pale vein-feathering patterns; some infected plants show no symptoms.
care: Record symptom patterns, inspect planting material, and clean vine-cutting tools. Seek confirmation for suspected virus symptoms.
prevention: Use pathogen-tested clean planting material and keep nursery stock away from affected crops.
limitations: A photo cannot confirm a virus. Absence of visible symptoms does not establish virus-free status.

name: Sweetpotato weevil
cues: Ant-like adult weevils or small holes and tunnels in storage roots or vines; damage alone can have other causes.
care: Keep storage roots covered with soil and inspect planting material and roots for weevils and tunneling.
prevention: Use clean planting material, rotate crops, and remove crop residues after harvest.
source: University of Florida IFAS Extension · Insect management for sweet potatoes
limitations: Prefer a close-up of the insect. Root holes alone do not confirm the pest species.
